rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah is one in essence, attributes, and names from every perspective; divinity belongs exclusively to Him as an intrinsically one reality.
rows.anchor: gerek zâtı, gerek sıfâtı, gerek esmâsı hangi nokta-i nazarla mülâhaza edilirse edilsin hep birdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowing God through many names and attributes does not imply multiplicity or a counterpart in His essence; knowing His unity does not impose a limit on Him.
rows.anchor: O’nun zâtında kesret veya zâtına bir nazîr isbat etmek mânasına olmayacağı gibi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine oneness is not numerical unity within plurality: ordinary counted units can be divided, multiplied, and matched, whereas God's unity excludes all such possibilities.
rows.anchor: ne içinde ne dışında kesir ve misil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Multiplicity belongs to created things and God's dominion; creatures are relations that exist and disappear by His command.
rows.anchor: onun halk sıfatına râci‘olan mahlûkātında, mülkündedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The countable unit is the relative first in a number sequence, can have multiples, and is only metaphorically called a number itself; it is not God's true unity.
rows.anchor: Buna aded, sayı demek mecaz olsa da aded yolunda vâhid demek hakikattir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God First means that He has no predecessor, and calling Him Last means that He has no successor; the names should be said together.
rows.anchor: O’na “Evvel” demek ikincisi var demek değil, sâbıkı yok demektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God the beginning of a count is wrong: He is not the starting point of a second like Himself; the revealed names are Mubdi and Mu'id, not Mebde'.
rows.anchor: esmâ-i hüsnâda “mebde’” ismi vârid olmamıştır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God remains one and alone in every respect, as expressed by the report that He existed with nothing alongside Him and is as He was.
rows.anchor: O her nokta-i nazardan bir, hep bir, hep tektir

rows.speaker: İmâm-ı A‘zam
rows.claim: In Fiqh al-Akbar, Abu Hanifa explains God's oneness as having no partner, rather than as numerical unity.
rows.anchor: Allah teâlâ مِنْ حَيْثُ الْعَدَدِ değil, مِنْ حَيْثُ أَنَّهُ لاَ شَرِيكَ لَهُ وَاحِدٌ

rows.speaker: Sâhib-Keşşâf
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari glosses ahad as having no second, whether implicitly within God or externally alongside Him.
rows.anchor: ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ “lâ sâniye leh”, yani “ikincisi yok” diye tefsir eylemiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators generally caution that God's oneness here does not mean one by numerical counting.
rows.anchor: Bütün tefsirler de aded tarîkiyle vâhid demek olmadığına tenbih eylemişlerdir

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: Razi says knowing God is a present paradise: paradise is attaining what accords with one's intellect and desire, and the grave is no prison for a believer whose wishes are met there.
rows.anchor: Ma‘rifetullah, cennet-i hâzıradır. Zira cennet senin aklına ve arzuna muvâfık olana nâil olmandır

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: Razi compares reason to an ambitious servant who submits only to its Lord, while appetite resembles a dependent seeking gifts from a rich benefactor.
rows.anchor: Akıl himmet-i âliye sâhibi bir insan gibidir, mevlâsından başkasına münkād olmaz

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: Reason seeks God to thank Him for past gifts, while desire seeks God in hope of future gifts; each embraces Him as knowing and rich.
rows.anchor: Akıl geçmiş nimetlere şükretmek için mevlâsını tanımak ister

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: Doubt unsettles reason and appetite by asking whether another equal or another source of help exists, driving the mind into inquiry for certainty.
rows.anchor: Belki O’nun bir misli de vardır! Ve ey şehvet! Yalnız O’na nasıl bağlandın?

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: God sends His Messenger to guide the servant and preserve the pleasure of worship and gratitude, revealing the truthful declaration of divine oneness to spare arduous inference.
rows.anchor: Resûlünü göndermiş ve ona ‘kendinden söyleme, Benim doğrudan doğru sâdık olarak bildiğim şu kelâmımı söyle’ diyerek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Samed has two main lexical explanations: the one to whom aim and need are directed, and the complete, solid being with no hollow or deficiency.
rows.anchor: “Samed” ismi hakkında lügat nokta-i nazarından mülâhaza olunacak esaslı iki mâna mervîdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first sense derives from samd, to aim straight toward an object; a people's samed is its highest chief and refuge in affairs and needs.
rows.anchor: kasd doğrudan doğru kendisine müteveccih olan maksud mânasına olmaktır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second sense describes something with no cavity, void, gap, or penetration, like the Turkish word som for solid and whole.
rows.anchor: hiç cevfi, boşluğu olmayan, eksiksiz gediksiz, deliksiz, nüfûz edilmez şeye denir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The solid sense also carries purity and permanence; samed is linked to stopping or plugging, as with a bottle stopper, and can mean one who neither hungers nor thirsts.
rows.anchor: Şişenin tıkacına “sımad” denilmesi de bundandır

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi reports that some later lexicographers called a smooth stone that admits no dust or intrusion samed, comparable to a som stone.
rows.anchor: Râzî der ki: Ehl-i lügattan müteahhirînden bazısı toz kabul etmez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators take samed as a positive attribute from the first sense; some report the negative attribute from the second, and some include both.
rows.anchor: Müfessirlerin ekserîsi tâ yukarıda da işaret olunduğu üzere birinci mânadan olarak sıfat-ı sübûtiye

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fullest interpretation joins the two senses through their highest necessary implications, rather than directly intending both literal homonymous meanings at once.
rows.anchor: en lâyıkı da budur

rows.speaker: İbn Cerîr, Mücâhid, Hasan ve İkrime
rows.claim: They explain samed as having no cavity.
rows.anchor: İbn Cerîr Mücâhid’den ve Hasan’dan ve İkrime’den “samed, lâ-cevfe leh” demektir

rows.speaker: Sa‘îd b. Müseyyeb
rows.claim: He explains samed as having no internal organs.
rows.anchor: Sa‘îd b. Müseyyeb’den, “ahşâsı yok” diye

rows.speaker: Şa‘bî
rows.claim: He explains samed as one who neither eats nor drinks.
rows.anchor: Şa‘bî’den, “yemez içmez” diye

rows.speaker: İkrime
rows.claim: One report from Ikrima says nothing comes out from God.
rows.anchor: yine İkrime’den ve daha bazılarından da kendisinden bir şey hurûc etmez

rows.speaker: Abdullah b. Büreyde
rows.claim: The author calls this the strongest transmitted report: Ibn Burayda attributes to the Prophet the definition that samed has no cavity.
rows.anchor: Abdullah b. Büreyde’nin “her hâlde Peygamber’e ref‘etmiştir, biliyorum, اَلصَّمَدُ الَّذِي لاَ جَوْفَ لَه’dir dedi”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turkish som, whole, gapless, and solid express the word; the sense also implies complete self-sufficiency and supreme perfection.
rows.anchor: Türkçemizde bu mânalar “eksiksiz, gediksiz, deliksiz, som” diye ifade olunabilir

rows.speaker: Ebü’l-Âliye ve Muhammed b. Ka‘b
rows.claim: They say samed means the one described as neither begetting nor begotten.
rows.anchor: Ebü’l-Âliye ve Muhammed b. Ka‘b gibi bazıları da لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ bunun mânası olduğunu söylemişler

rows.speaker: Rebî‘ b. Enes
rows.claim: He says no affliction can befall God.
rows.anchor: Rebî‘b. Enes’ten “kendisine âfât[^9] ârız olmaz”

rows.speaker: Mukātil b. Hayyan
rows.claim: He says God has no flaw or deficiency.
rows.anchor: Mukātil b. Hayyan’dan[^10]“kendisinde hiç ayıp ve eksiklik olmayan”

rows.speaker: İbn Keysan
rows.claim: He says God is not characterized by any attribute of created beings.
rows.anchor: İbn Keysan’dan “mahlûkāttan hiçbirinin sıfatıyla tavsif olunmaz”

rows.speaker: Hasan ve Katâde
rows.claim: They interpret samed as everlasting and enduring, never passing away.
rows.anchor: Hasan’dan ve Katâde’den mervî olduğu üzere bazıları da “lem yezel ve lâ yezâl, fâni olmaz bâkī, dâim” demişlerdir

rows.speaker: İbn Enbârî
rows.claim: He says lexicographers agree that samed is the chief to whom people turn directly for needs and affairs, with no superior.
rows.anchor: Ehl-i lügat beyninde samed, ‘nâsın havâic ve umûrunda kendisine samd eder

rows.speaker: Zeccâc
rows.claim: He defines samed as the one to whom sovereignty culminates, on whom everything depends, and whom everything makes its goal and refuge.
rows.anchor: Zeccâc da demiştir ki: “‘Samed’ su’dud[^13], yani ululuk kendisine müntehî olan

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas defines samed as perfect in sovereignty, honor, greatness, forbearance, knowledge, wisdom, and every kind of nobility.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas’tan şöyle rivayet eylemiştir: “‘Samed’ su’dudünde[^16] kâmil olan seyyid ve şerefinde kâmil olan şerîf

rows.speaker: Ebû Hüreyre
rows.claim: He says everyone needs God while God needs no one.
rows.anchor: Ebû Hüreyre’den: “اَلْمُسْتـَغْنِي عَنْ كُلِّ أَحَدٍ، اَلْمُحْتَاجُ إِلَيْهِ كُلُّ أَحَدٍ herkesten müstağnî

rows.speaker: Sa‘îd b. Cübeyr
rows.claim: He defines samed as perfect in every attribute and act.
rows.anchor: Sa‘îd b. Cübeyr’den: [6308] “Bütün sıfât ve ef‘âlinde kâmil”

rows.speaker: Süddî
rows.claim: He says God is sought for desires and invoked for calamities.
rows.anchor: Süddî’den: “Regāibde maksud, mesâibde müstegās”

rows.speaker: Ca‘fer-i Sâdık
rows.claim: He defines samed as the unconquered victor.
rows.anchor: Ca‘fer-i Sâdık’tan: “Gālib-i gayr-i mağlub”

rows.speaker: Hüseyin b. Fudayl
rows.claim: He says God's judgment and will cannot be followed or overturned.
rows.anchor: Hüseyin b. Fudayl’dan: “يَحْكُمُ مَا يُرِيدُ وَيـَفْعَلُ مَا يَشَاءُ hükmünü tâkip edecek yok

rows.speaker: İbn Cerîr Ebû Ca‘fer Taberî
rows.claim: Tabari says the familiar Arabic meaning is a chief with no superior to whom people direct their needs.
rows.anchor: Arap indinde ‘samed’ اَلسَّيِّدُ الَّذِي يُصْمَدُ إِلَيْهِ الَّذِي لاَ أَحَدَ فـَوْقَهُ’dır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet's phrase al-sayyid al-samad supports the familiar Arabic sense of the supreme chief sought by others.
rows.anchor: بِعَمْرِو بْنِ مَسْعُودٍ وَبِالسَّيِّدِ الصَّمَدْ

rows.speaker: Zibrikan
rows.claim: His verse also uses samed for a lord or chief, supporting the lexical sense of supreme leadership.
rows.anchor: Zibrikan[^20] da وَلاَ رَهِينَةَ إِلاَّ سَيِّدٌ صَمَدُ demiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best interpretation is the meaning familiar in the language of Qur'an's revelation; if Ibn Burayda's prophetic report is sound, it would outrank other views because the Prophet knows God's intent best.
rows.anchor: kelimenin tevilinde evlâ olan Kur’ân’ın nâzil olduğu lisanda mâruf olan mânadır

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib defines samed as the chief to whom one directs oneself in an affair and notes its sense of aiming straight toward him.
rows.anchor: Râgıb da der ki: “‘Samed’ emirde masmûd-i ileyh olan seyyiddir

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib says non-hollow beings include both beings below humans and beings above them, such as the Creator and angels.
rows.anchor: ecvef olmayan ise iki şeydir. Birisi insandan dûndur, birisi de a‘lâdır: Bârî ve melâike gibi

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib says al-Samad contrasts with those whom some people deify; the statement that Jesus and his mother ate food points to their creaturely need.
rows.anchor: ‘Allâhu’s-samed’ kavliyle maksad da o birtakımlarının ilâhlık isnad ettikleri kimselerin hilâfına olduğuna tenbihtir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Christians attributed divinity to Jesus and his mother, so the Qur'an points to their needs and bodily events to show that they cannot be gods.
rows.anchor: Nasârâ Hazret-i Îsâ’ya ve anasına ilâhlık isnad etmişlerdi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who favor the no-cavity, no-eating sense do so partly because it signals God's freedom from need, a point made explicit by that gloss.
rows.anchor: “Lâ-cevfe leh, yemez içmez” diye

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Having no cavity or need can imply positive perfection, but it does not itself explicitly state that God fulfills all needs and is everyone's refuge.
rows.anchor: kendi eksiği, ihtiyâcı olmamak, muhtaç olanların hâcetlerini bitirmek ve işlerinde merci‘ve maksudları olmak yüksekliğini tasrih etmiş olmaz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The familiar first meaning directly establishes God as the refuge and goal of all needs while also implying the perfection and lack of deficiency conveyed by the second.
rows.anchor: Evvelki mâna ise bunu tasrih etmekle sıfât-ı sübûtiye kemâlâtını müstelzim olduğu gibi

rows.speaker: Sâhib-Keşşâf
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari parses samed as the sought chief in needs and says the Creator is the one every creature seeks and needs, while He needs none.
rows.anchor: O, tanıdığınız, gökleri ve yeri ve sizleri yaratan hâlıkınız diye ikrar ettiğiniz Allah’tır

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina defines complete self-sufficiency as having no dependence on anything external for essence or intrinsic perfection; neediness in these would make one poor, not truly self-sufficient.
rows.anchor: Tam ganî zâtında, ve zâtından mütemekkin olduğu sıfâtında

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Dependence in purely relational attributes does not impair complete self-sufficiency, since the need belongs to the other party, not God.
rows.anchor: Zira bunlarda fakir olan o

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not need creatures or the world; creatures and the world need Him, and He completes them without being completed by them.
rows.anchor: O hâlık olmak için mahlûka muhtaç değil, mahluk O’na muhtaçtır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Benefits and wisdoms may result from God's acts for creatures, but they are not final causes or purposes needed by God.
rows.anchor: onların hiçbirisi O’nun için illet-i gāiye, garaz değildir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Complete self-sufficiency is also defined as accepting no change in one's essence.
rows.anchor: “gınâ-yı tâm”, zâtında hiçbir tegayyür kabul etmeyendir

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: Ibn Arabi describes Samadiyya as the refuge where every needy person turns because what they need lies in its treasures.
rows.anchor: Bu hazret ilticâ ve istinad hazretindendir ki, herhangi bir emre muhtaç olan her fakir ona ilticâ eyler

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: Ibn Arabi asks whether this refuge's sufficiency is God's essential independence, invoking the verse that God is independent of the worlds.
rows.anchor: Onda غَنِيٌّ عَنِ الْعَالَم۪ينَ [^33] فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ [Âl-i İmrân 3/97] buyurulan gınâ-yı nefsî var mı yok mu?

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: Ibn Arabi says God's treasuries contain all things, as stated in the verse about treasuries with God.
rows.anchor: Nitekim وَإِن مِّن شَىْءٍ إِلَّا عِندَنَا خَزَآئِنُهُۥ [el-Hicr 15/21] vârid olmuştur

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: The divine treasures are fixed known things that God knows and sees, bringing into existence whatever He wills and leaving whatever He wills.
rows.anchor: onlardan dilediğini vücûda çıkarır ve dilediğini bırakır

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: Although called treasuries, their contents are not finite; needy thoughts concern things held there that seek to appear in existence.
rows.anchor: onlarda hasr u tenâhî tahayyül olunur, hâlbuki gayr-i mütenâhîdirler

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: Existing things remain dependent on God for what has not yet been created, and can serve as means through which another receives what it needs.
rows.anchor: mevcut olan, o hazinedekine, vücûda iftikārı hususunda muîn gibidir

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: The world is a chain of treasuries and transfers, but all things remain with God; only God is the ultimate refuge for affairs.
rows.anchor: umûrda ilticâ ve istinad olunacak samed ancak O’dur

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: Some rely on God and others on causes, but causes often betray those who trust them, whereas God saves those who entrust their affairs to Him.
rows.anchor: esbâb kendilerine itimad ve ilticâ edenlere çok [6312] vakitlerde hıyanet eder

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: People have a share in samediyya because newly acquired knowledge of God appears through them, making them the relative object of divine seeking in that act of knowing.
rows.anchor: Allah’a ma‘rifet-i hâdise ancak seninle olur

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: The Prophet instructed worshippers to offset a prayer screen to one side instead of facing it directly; Ibn Arabi reads this as forbidding direct ultimate aim toward anything besides God.
rows.anchor: لاَ تَصْمُدْ إِلَيْهِ صَمْدًا ona samden, yani sütreye doğrudan doğru düpedüz kasd ve teveccüh etmeyesin

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: A prayer screen is a means: turning it to the right signals a strong cause and to the left a weak one, but reliance and direct intention must remain with God.
rows.anchor: Sütre sebeptir, sağ ile sebeb-i kavîye, sol ile de sebeb-i za‘îfe tenbih eylemiştir

rows.speaker: Muhyiddîn-i Arabî
rows.claim: Ibn Arabi says the person touched by divine inspiration relies weakly on causes and directs the complete aim only toward God.
rows.anchor: dosdoğru samd ü kasdı ancak Allah’adır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Arabi's explanation is a valuable admonition: knowledge and human duty must have no ultimate aim besides God, and samed means refuge and reliance, implying needlessness.
rows.anchor: insanlık marifet ve vazifesinin Hak’tan başka hedefi olmamak lâzım geldiğini tebârüz ettirmek itibariyle cidden güzel nasihattir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account overlooks God's essential self-sufficiency, the negative attribute stated in the verse that God is independent of the worlds.
rows.anchor: Birisi gınâda وَاللهُ غَنِيٌّ عَنِ الْعَالَمِينَ mantûkunca sıfat-ı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It considers positive sufficiency through divine treasuries yet seems to treat possession of one or several needed things as sufficient for samediyya.
rows.anchor: muhtaç olunan şeylerden birine veya birkaçına mâlik olmak samediyet mefhûmunun sübûtu için kâfi imiş gibi göstermiş olmasıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Samediyya means being the ultimate refuge in every need, not merely an object sought for some needs; the lexical definitions stress having no superior and sovereignty's culmination.
rows.anchor: samediyet bazı hâcette maksud ve mültecâ olmak değil, bütün hâcâtta müntehâ olarak maksud ve mültecâ olmaktır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without essential independence there is no complete generosity or dignity: one could be defeated, deprived, or destroyed, and could not be the ultimate object of reliance.
rows.anchor: gınâ-yı nefsîsi olmayanda tam izzet bulunmaz, mağlub edilmek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra's report explicitly states complete independence, and al-Kashshaf and Ibn Sina also point to it.
rows.anchor: Ebû Hüreyre’den rivayette اَلْمُسْتـَغْنِي عَنْ كُلِّ أَحَدٍ، اَلْمُحْتَاجُ إِلَيْهِ كُلُّ أَحَدٍ diye istiğnâ-yı tâm tasrih olunduğu gibi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Arabi intended a relative, nonabsolute share of samediyya in creation and causes, which can serve as evidence for knowing God; ordinary usage can call such a thing samed.
rows.anchor: hazâin-i ilâhiyeden olan ve ma‘rifet-i hâdise ile Allah’ı tanımak için delâil-i Hak’tan bulunan kevn ve esbâb âleminde

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God is the complete Samad; causes may be used, but they betray reliance, and total trust and direct intention must not be attached to anything besides God.
rows.anchor: Esbâb, itimad edenlere çok vakitlerde hıyanet [6315] eder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite predicate al-Samad can express restriction: if the article is generic, the whole class belongs to God; if externally definite, it points to the uniquely recognized highest Samad.
rows.anchor: müsnedin ma‘rife olması da kasr ifade eder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name samed may be applied to others in some ordinary sense, but al-Samad in its perfect sense and with divine oneness belongs to God.
rows.anchor: ancak “es-Samed” ekmel mânasıyla ve ehadiyet vasfıyla muttasıf olarak Allah’ın esmâsından ve O’na mahsus olur

rows.speaker: İbn Esîr
rows.claim: Ibn Athir summarizes samed as the supreme chief at whom sovereignty ends, the enduring one, the one without a cavity, and the one sought in needs.
rows.anchor: “Allah teâlâ’nın esmâsında es-Samed: Su’dud

rows.speaker: Hazret-i Ömer
rows.claim: An example quoted from Umar warns listeners against learning genealogies and using them to disparage others.
rows.anchor: Hazret-i Ömer’in şu hadîsi de ondandır: إِيَّاكُمْ وَتـَعَلُّمَ الأَْنَسَابِ والطَّعْنَ فِيهَا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umar's use shows samed can be an indefinite human title for a supreme chief; Ibn Arabi invokes such relative use while reserving absolute samediyya for God.
rows.anchor: Hazret-i Ömer’in kelâmında “samed” nekre olarak insanlar hakkında da kullanılmıştır

rows.speaker: Muaz b. Cemuh
rows.claim: In the report about Abu Jahl's killing, he says he aimed at him and waited for his moment of inattention.
rows.anchor: فَصَمَدْتُ لَهُ حَتَّى أَمْكَنَتْنِي مِنْهُ غِرَّةٌ

rows.speaker: Hazret-i Ali
rows.claim: Ali's exhortation samdan samda means to aim or proceed steadily until the pillar of truth appears.
rows.anchor: فَصَمْداً صَمْداً حَتَّى يـَتَجَلَّى لَكُمْ عَمُودُ الْحَقِّ

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi reports up to eighteen interpretations of samed based on its positive and negative lexical senses, including transcendence from diminution, change, and temporal or spatial containment.
rows.anchor: on sekiz mânaya kadar tefsir ettiklerini

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi considers it possible to include all meanings: necessary existence entails divine negations, and being creator of all entails all divine attributes.
rows.anchor: ‘es-samed’ lafzının bütün bu mânaların hepsine hamlidir

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: If samed is the ultimate object of needs and unchanging in essence, no other being can be samed, and the verse establishes that there is no god besides Allah.
rows.anchor: İkinci mesele de: ‘Allâhu’ssamed’ demek vücudda Allah’tan mâ‘adâ bir samed

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi takes verse 112:1 to deny composition in God's essence and verse 112:2 to deny partners, equals, and opposites.
rows.anchor: ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ zâtında hiçbir vechile ne terkib ne telif bulunmamak mânasına bir olduğuna işaret

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi asks why ahad is indefinite while al-Samad is definite; one answer says ahad is effectively definite because in negation and counting it applies only to God, unlike samed.
rows.anchor: Nefy ve adedin gayride ‘ehad’ Allah’tan başkasına ıtlak edilmediğinden dolayı ma‘rife hükmünde

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi says ordinary people regard every existent as sensible and divisible, so indivisible oneness is unfamiliar, while the idea of a sought refuge is familiar, as 43:87 illustrates.
rows.anchor: her mevcud mahsüstür, hâlbuki her mahsüsün münkasim olduğu sâbittir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalili's better explanation is that polytheists recognized Allah but not His unity, sought different needs from multiple gods, and failed to see that the ultimate deity must be one.
rows.anchor: Müşrikler, Allah’ı ve ulûhiyetini tanıyorlarsa da O’nun ulûhiyette birliğini, ehadiyetini tanımıyorlardı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Polytheists knew a deity was the highest object of worship but did not see that all goals and needs converge on the one creator; their divided objects of worship caused conflict.
rows.anchor: nizâ‘[^67] ve şikāk içinde yüzüyorlardı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their shock at the declaration of one God is illustrated by their objection that many gods were made into one god.
rows.anchor: أَجَعَلَ ٱلْءَالِهَةَ إِلَٰهًا وَٰحِدًا إِنَّ هَٰذَا لَشَىْءٌ عُجَابٌ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun of the affair introduces an important truth they do not know: Allah is one; ahad is indefinite to announce that unfamiliar fact.
rows.anchor: هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ diye “ehad” nekre olarak haber verilmiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite al-Samad reassures people that every need and diverse goal is met in the complete, solid, self-sufficient refuge, God alone.
rows.anchor: hasr ifade etmek için lâm-ı ta‘rîf ile ٱللَّهُ ٱلصَّمَدُ buyurulmuştur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Samed should be understood through its familiar lexical senses and their highest positive and negative implications, not by directly combining both homonymous definitions.
rows.anchor: lafz-ı müştereki her iki mânasına birden haml suretiyle umûm-ı müşterek olarak değil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators differ on calling God sayyid; a sound hadith says that Allah is the true master, while Suhayli advises against attaching a genitive phrase such as master of angels to God.
rows.anchor: Süheylî demiştir ki: “Muzâf olarak Allah’a ‘seyyid’ ıtlak edilmez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Turkish, Allah is not called efendimiz; titles such as seyyidü'l-halk and seyyid-i kâinat refer to the Messenger.
rows.anchor: Lisânımızda “Allah efendimiz” denmez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All beings naturally or intentionally turn toward God for the realization of possible perfections; He is both origin and goal, First and Last.
rows.anchor: Allah teâlâ hem mübdi‘-i kül, hem gāye-i küldür, onun için Evvel ü Âhir’dir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired verses signal that origin and final goal converge in divine oneness.
rows.anchor: bu iki âyette bu iki noktanın ehadiyet-i ilâhiyede birleştiğine tenbih vardır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating Allah allows one predicate to be indefinite and the other definite; without repetition both predicates would need the same definiteness.
rows.anchor: haberlerin birinin nekre, birinin ma‘rife olarak getirilmesindeki fâideyi temindir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two predicates are each independently intended as information, so no conjunction is used.
rows.anchor: İki haberden ikisinin de doğrudan doğru maksûd bi’l-ifâde olduklarına tenbihtir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each of ahad and al-Samad independently identifies the essence, so the second predicate does not use a pronoun in place of repeating Allah.
rows.anchor: “Ehad”, “es-Samed” vasıflarından her birinin ta‘yîn-i zâtta müstakil olduklarına tenbihtir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ahad comes first because polytheists first needed to learn oneness; al-Samad answers the question it raises and follows as its proof or consequence.
rows.anchor: müşriklere karşı evvelemirde ehadiyeti bildirmek ehem

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only the one who is completely self-sufficient can be the ultimate refuge while all else depends on Him; oneness entails complete self-sufficiency.
rows.anchor: ehadiyet samediyeti, gınâ-yı tâmmı müstelzim olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second clause functions in part as evidence and in part as result, as an independent or reinforcing sentence.
rows.anchor: bu cümle min vechin delil ve min vechin netice gibi olarak cümle-i müste’nife veya müekkidedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening affirms all majesty and beauty in God's divinity, then His absolute unity without composition or likeness, and His essential independence while all creatures need Him.
rows.anchor: Hâsılı Hak teâlâ evvelâ her vechile samd ve tâzim hakkı olan bütün celâl ve cemâl sıfatlarını câmi‘ulûhiyetini

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial of begetting rejects claims that God has daughters or a son, that angels are His daughters or Jesus His son, or that another shares His divine essence.
rows.anchor: O’na hâşâ[^79] tenâsül isnad edenlerin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lam yalid means God did not beget and did not separate any part of His own essence; He is neither father nor mother.
rows.anchor: O doğurmadı kendisinden, kendi zâtından bir cüz çıkarmadı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Begetting would require a new like-kind part to form and separate, implying composition, origination, need, division, change, and mortality; offspring share the parent's kind.
rows.anchor: Doğurmak O’nda O’na mücânis yeni bir cüz’ün teşekkülüyle O’ndan infisal iktizâ eyler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reproduction serves the survival of mortal species and may be a perfection for needy mortals, but it is deficiency for the self-sufficient God who contains every perfection.
rows.anchor: doğurmak, yerine kalacak evlâdı, nesli olmak, muhtaç fâniler için maksud bir kemâl olsa da

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has no parts, matter, genus, species, likeness, need, or deficiency; He creates whatever possibilities He wills by the simple command Be.
rows.anchor: Allah teâlâ ehad, samed olduğu için tecezzî etmez, O’ndan ne bir cüz ne bir cevher ne bir madde kopup ayrılmaz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation is not a piece of God's own being emanating or being born; God brings what is nonexistent into existence by creation, as 3:47 states.
rows.anchor: O’ndan sudûr ve tevellüd tarîkiyle değil, ma‘dûmu ibdâ‘ve îcad etmesi suretiyle olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Possibility cannot arise without a cause; every change or origination requires an agent, and reason necessarily seeks an efficient cause for every event.
rows.anchor: vücudda herhangi bir tegayyür ve hudûs gerek tekâmüle, tezâyüde, gerek tenâkusa doğru herhangi bir değişiklik bi’z-zarûre bir illete delâlet eyler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A true efficient cause creates and originates its effect; begetting presupposes prior creation, and a parent is only the locus or passage of birth, not its ultimate cause.
rows.anchor: Hakīkī illet-i fâiliye ise ma‘lûlünü doğurmaz, yok iken ibdâ‘eder, halkeder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Polytheists confused creation with begetting and attributed procreation to God, including a lineage between God and angels, jinn, or devils, as 37:101-102 and 37:158 indicate.
rows.anchor: yaratmakla doğurmayı fark edemediklerinden dolayı illiyet kanununu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The later Christian doctrine of Father, Holy Spirit, and Son wrongly attributes offspring and procreative need to God; the author points to 2:116-117 and 5:72-73.
rows.anchor: sonraki Hıristiyanlığın ulûhiyeti Baba, Rûhu’lkudüs, Oğul diye tevâlüd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial of begetting also denies the notion that Jesus was extracted from God's divine substance, made a god like Him, or shares divinity through a common essence.
rows.anchor: kendisinin Allahlık cevherinden çıkardı, kendisi gibi ilâh yaptı
